title: The Offensive Begins
subtitle: Opening operations of Operation Typhoon.
author: Robert M. Dobo
summary: Guderian opens Typhoon’s southern attack as German concentration, Soviet defence and negotiations for supplies test the prospect of a short war.
body:
An offensive with two beginnings

On 30 September 1941, Heinz Guderian's Second Panzer Group attacked towards Orel from the southern side of the forces assembling for Operation Typhoon. The main assault by Fedor von Bock's Army Group Centre would follow on 2 October. The staggered opening reflected the operation's scale: separate mobile forces had to reach positions from which they could turn behind the Soviet armies protecting Moscow. Germany was attempting another vast encirclement after its victory at Kiev. Its commanders expected the destruction of those field armies to open the way to a decisive result, but the first thrust began before the whole operation could be brought to bear. [1][2]

The victory at Kiev had made a renewed concentration against Moscow possible, but the formations returning to the central theatre carried the consequences of the earlier campaign. Men and vehicles had travelled and fought for months; the move north required another expenditure before the next battle began. Behind them, occupation continued to expose civilians to German persecution. The Babyn Yar massacre, begun on 29 September, continued on the day Guderian attacked. These events shared the campaign's geography without becoming the same operation. Germany was extending its military effort while the institutions following its conquests were already using their power against people who could no longer escape them. [1][3]

The question for this chapter is therefore narrower and more revealing than whether Germany was “close” to Moscow. What could an army group actually bring to bear after three months of fighting, and what did its leaders expect a new encirclement to accomplish? The German high command was not simply ordering every unit to race for the capital's towers. It intended to break the Soviet field armies guarding the approaches, opening the route to Moscow and weakening the state's capacity to continue the war. German operational plans, Soviet defences and the material means of moving both armies made that prospect uncertain even before the first vehicles ran into autumn rain.[1]

What the German command sought

Hitler's Directive 35, issued on 6 September, restored the central army group to the role of principal striking force. The order followed a bitter argument over objectives. During August, German armour had been diverted from the direct approach to Moscow towards the Ukraine, while another transfer supported operations in the north. Those decisions contributed to the destruction of the Soviet Southwestern Front around Kiev. They also meant that the formations now expected to fight in the centre had to be recalled, repaired and supplied. A decision on a map was not the same as a division ready at its starting line.[1]

The plan that emerged aimed first at the Soviet forces standing west of Moscow. German panzer groups were to penetrate on both sides of the defenders and meet beyond them; infantry armies would help widen the breaches and reduce the forces trapped inside. The northern and central mobile arms were directed towards the Vyazma area, while Guderian's southern formation moved towards the approaches to Orel and Bryansk. The precise commands and their movements will become the subject of the 2 October study. For 30 September, the essential point is that the German design required the synchronised destruction of several Soviet formations before an advance on Moscow could be treated as an accomplished fact.[1][2]

The German planning study shows how much movement lay behind the apparently simple arrows. Fourth Panzer Group's projected striking force near Roslavl included the 10th Panzer Division already in the area, two divisions assigned from army reserve, one from Army Group South and two from Army Group North. The northern concentration near Velizh under Third Panzer Group likewise drew on formations from the Leningrad sector. Guderian's group was to turn from its Ukrainian operations with five panzer divisions assigned to the wide southern sweep. These were proposed concentrations and roles, not proof that every listed division was present at full strength or had crossed its start line on 30 September. The transfers required lengthy lateral journeys and consumed transport that would soon be needed for the offensive itself.[2]

The operational language concealed a strategic wager. Germany had destroyed or captured enormous Soviet forces since June, yet the Soviet state had continued to raise armies, move industry and resist on separate fronts. German planners still hoped that another battle of annihilation would do what the earlier ones had failed to do: end organised resistance in the decisive theatre. The intended capture or isolation of Moscow mattered because the city was a governmental centre, a transport hub and a powerful symbol. But those were different kinds of value. Occupying a capital, cutting its rail connections, destroying an army west of it and forcing a government to capitulate were not interchangeable outcomes. The plan assumed that success in the first of these steps would help bring the others within reach.[1]

Army Group Centre's strength on paper has sometimes encouraged an easy description of overwhelming superiority. The U.S. Army history gives approximately 1.929 million men for the German army group and at least 1.25 million for the three Soviet fronts opposite it, but warns that the German total included a substantial auxiliary component. It judges the effective strength of the German combat divisions a much closer match. Stahel's published introduction likewise describes the exceptional concentration of divisions assembled for Typhoon while stressing the distance between operational victory and the hoped-for strategic end to the war. These figures are useful only when their categories remain visible. A man attached to a supply organisation, a rifleman in a front-line battalion and a wounded soldier carried on a roll do not represent the same immediate combat power. Neither aggregate tells us how many tanks could move that morning, how much fuel reached them or where the opposing forces were concentrated.[1][4]

Reading the numbers

The German and Soviet totals in many accounts count different kinds of personnel and were assembled by different institutions. The German army group's large aggregate included auxiliaries; the Soviet number covered three fronts. Use them to frame the scale of the battle, not to derive a precise odds ratio for the fighting on 30 September.[1]

The southern arm moves

Guderian's command had only recently been central to the Kiev encirclement. In August, his Second Panzer Group moved south from Army Group Centre's sector; in September its armoured spearheads met those of Ewald von Kleist's First Panzer Group east of Kiev. That success did not place Guderian's men back on the Moscow axis by magic. The distance travelled south, the fighting in Ukraine and the subsequent turn north all had to be absorbed by machines, crews and supply columns. When the southern wing attacked on 30 September, it began from a position shaped by the preceding campaign, not from a fresh reserve assembled behind an untouched front.[1][2]

The immediate movement was towards Orel, a junction whose roads and railways connected the approaches to Bryansk and the country farther east. Guderian's thrust sought to cut into the southern side of the Soviet defensive system and prevent Bryansk Front from dealing with the northern arm as an intact force. That purpose is clearer than a story told only in kilometres of advance. An armoured column could pass a town or cross a line and still leave Soviet units fighting behind it. An operational breakthrough became strategically useful only if the army could support it, keep its roads open and exploit the disruption before Soviet commanders established a new line.[2][1]

Eremenko's Bryansk Front stood between Guderian and the southern approaches to Moscow. Formed during the summer crisis, it had already confronted the consequences of the German turn towards Kiev. Its task now was to contain a mobile force that could threaten its flank and communications as well as attack its positions. Eremenko still commanded armies capable of fighting; their eventual encirclement was not a condition that existed before the attack. The opening German success would depend on breaking their connections quickly enough to prevent an orderly withdrawal or a coordinated response. That made the direction of Guderian's movement as important as the ground he gained. [1]

Guderian's formation was still called Second Panzer Group on 30 September; the designation Second Panzer Army followed on 5 October. Here the earlier name matters because it identifies the command that opened the offensive. The mobile groups were instruments for deep penetration, but their success depended on infantry armies following behind. Tanks could disrupt a Soviet headquarters or seize a crossing before slower formations arrived. They could not simultaneously guard every road, receive masses of prisoners and maintain a continuous front. The opening operation therefore placed a premium on cooperation between commanders whose formations moved at different speeds and whose immediate priorities could diverge. [2][1]

The demand for fuel shows how preparation for Typhoon extended beyond the assembly areas. German planners calculated that petroleum trains entering the eastern theatre would have to increase from twenty-two a day to twenty-seven between 17 September and 2 October, then to twenty-nine from 3 October. These were requirements, not a record that the railway delivered every scheduled train. They nevertheless expose the offensive's dependence on an enlarged flow from the rear before the main attack even began. Stocks had been depleted, and incoming fuel was often being issued immediately. Concentrating tanks around Moscow meant concentrating consumption as well as striking power, while the other army groups continued to demand their share. An interruption behind the front could therefore matter before a spearhead encountered a new Soviet position.[2]

The defenders west of Moscow

The Soviet defence facing the central army group was not a single wall extending neatly across the map. Ivan Konev's Western Front held the principal western approaches; the Reserve Front under Semyon Budenny occupied positions farther back and in related sectors; Eremenko's Bryansk Front covered the southern danger. Their combined strength represented substantial Soviet mobilisation after the summer disasters. It did not mean that every division was equally prepared, that all sectors had adequate antitank weapons or that the three front headquarters could respond to a fast-moving encirclement as a unified instrument. An army's existence in the order of battle and its power at the point of contact are separate questions.[1]

The interval before Typhoon had allowed Soviet commanders to replenish forces and prepare positions west of Moscow. Those preparations gave the defenders real military resources, but depth also created a command problem. Forces deployed behind one another had to be able to support a threatened sector without abandoning another. If armour broke through between them, a rearward position could find the enemy approaching from an unexpected direction while neighbouring armies still faced west. German planning exploited precisely this vulnerability. The offensive sought to defeat the system linking Soviet armies together, so that troops who remained capable of fighting locally would lose the ability to act as a continuous front. [1]

The Stavka, the Soviet supreme command, had to distribute its attention among these approaches and the crises elsewhere. The loss of Kiev did not remove the need to defend Ukraine, and the threat to Leningrad did not disappear when Bock assembled his forces. Protecting Moscow therefore involved choices about which other demands could be met and which reserves could be spared. The Soviet concentration west of the capital was substantial, yet it could not be strengthened without regard to the rest of the war. Germany's ability to shift mobile formations between army groups had created an advantage in concentration; Soviet commanders now had to identify the main blow while those formations were beginning to move. [1]

The railways carried part of that strategic burden. Supplies and reinforcements had to move towards the front while industrial equipment and people moved away from threatened regions. Evacuation protected the possibility of future production at an immediate cost: a dismantled factory could not supply the next battle. Economic historian Mark Harrison stresses the interdependence of factories, power, materials and skilled labour. The Soviet government's problem was therefore larger than removing valuable machines. It had to preserve a working industrial system while continuing to equip armies whose needs could not be postponed until the machinery was installed again. Typhoon threatened to shorten the time available for both tasks. [5]

The material cost of a new beginning

The German plan demanded concentration at the very moment the army was most dispersed. Panzer formations had gone north and south, then were called back into Army Group Centre's operational design. Men could be reassigned by order; their vehicles had to cover the roads. Damaged engines, worn tracks and missing spare parts accumulated through months of movement and fighting. The mobile formations still possessed formidable striking power, but their operational endurance depended on maintenance and on fuel arriving behind the spearheads. An attack's first day could be impressive while the condition of its transport already limited the days that followed. The U.S. Army's reconstruction emphasises both the late-September reassembly and the gap between total personnel and effective combat power.[1][2]

Supply was also a geographic problem. Railways could move far more than trucks, but a train's usefulness depended on compatible track, working rolling stock, repair capacity and the distance from the railhead to a fighting unit. Once material left the train, a truck or horse cart had to carry it forward along roads shared with advancing troops, ambulances and rear-area traffic. A fast panzer group increased the distance its columns had to travel for every additional load of fuel or ammunition. Its apparent speed could therefore enlarge its own supply problem. These relationships were not unique to autumn, but they mattered more as the army tried to commit several mobile formations simultaneously rather than support a single local thrust.[2]

The German command possessed troubling evidence well before the October mud. An army-wide return of 4 September put only 47 percent of its tank strength in the eastern theatre in the category available for employment. Another 23 percent awaited repair, while 30 percent was disabled. These were earlier theatre totals, not the readiness of Guderian's force on the morning of the attack. Their importance lay in the warning they gave the planners. Repairs were restoring some vehicles, but replacement engines remained scarce, and machines already worn through the summer could fail again after relatively short journeys. The planning history describes emergency repairs that might extend a vehicle's life by only another 200–250 miles. German headquarters was committing a formidable force whose durability was much less reassuring than its concentration.[2]

The infantry's contribution was essential to the promised destruction of Soviet field forces. Once the panzer groups passed through a breach, infantry formations had to widen it, secure the route and prevent troops left behind from restoring the connection. Those tasks consumed ammunition and time even when the leading tanks met little opposition. The plan's success thus depended on two movements proceeding together: an advance into the Soviet rear and the consolidation of the corridor behind it. If either failed, a dramatic penetration could leave its own supply columns exposed. The German command was committing itself to a sequence of connected battles, not simply a race to a distant capital. [1]

Rail conversion offered a partial answer to the distance from German bases. By the end of September, the German planning history records that roughly 10,000 of the 15,000 miles of railway behind the front had been converted to the European gauge. That large engineering effort did not mean that every converted line could handle the required traffic. Locomotives, wagons, bridges, workshops and loading facilities still governed capacity, and supplies still had to reach the soldiers after leaving the train. The figures show both achievement and limitation: Germany had extended a transport network deep into Soviet territory, but its field armies were about to demand another expansion of the loads carried over it. [2]

Moscow asks what will arrive

While commanders prepared and opened the offensive, Soviet officials were negotiating for the means to survive a longer war. The British and American missions led by Lord Beaverbrook and W. Averell Harriman had arrived in Moscow on 28 September. Their meetings with Stalin were taking place as the German southern thrust began. Harriman's telegram transmitted on 30 September is valuable because it does not describe a triumphant coalition supplying everything Moscow required. It records a Soviet leader pressing for tanks and mobile antiaircraft and antitank weapons, with discussions of requirements still incomplete. Stalin's estimate of German superiority in tanks appears in the document as his belief, not as an independently established ratio.[6]

Stalin's requests illuminate the particular threats confronting Soviet troops. He wanted weapons that could accompany moving formations and stop armoured attacks, not simply greater quantities of any available equipment. A light tank with a cannon and adequate armour could serve a purpose that an unarmed vehicle could not; an antiaircraft gun that could move with troops answered a different need from a fixed installation. Harriman was recording a negotiation, so the requests cannot stand as a complete audit of Soviet deficiencies. They nevertheless identify the capabilities Stalin considered urgent while German armour was again being concentrated against his field armies. [6][1]

The negotiations also placed the offensive within a widening coalition war. Britain was already fighting Germany, while the United States was supplying countries resisting the Axis without yet being a belligerent in Europe. Their missions had come to discuss a continuing Soviet war effort. German planners, by contrast, hoped that the next encirclement would bring that effort to a decisive end. The difference was consequential: Soviet leaders were seeking resources beyond their own threatened industrial regions, and British and American officials were considering how to provide them. On 30 September the discussions remained unfinished, but they had already exposed the limits of a strategy that treated Soviet endurance as a purely domestic calculation. [6]

A request is not a delivery

Harriman's 30 September telegram records Stalin asking for light tanks, antitank weapons and antiaircraft guns. It also says the requirements discussion was unfinished. The conversation belongs in the history of the offensive because it reveals Soviet priorities, but it must not be counted as equipment already available to troops outside Moscow.[6]

Conquest and the people beneath it

Behind the forces turning towards Moscow, the consequences of the September conquest continued. At Babyn Yar, outside occupied Kiev, German perpetrators murdered 33,771 Jews on 29–30 September, according to the report used by the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum. Sonderkommando 4a, a unit of Einsatzgruppe C, carried out the massacre with German police support and assistance from local auxiliaries. The victims were civilians selected as Jews, not losses inflicted in Guderian's new attack. The distinction identifies the crime: conquest placed a community under German power, and the occupiers used that power to organise its murder. The two-day total belongs to the massacre as a whole, which was still taking place as the southern offensive began. [3]

Soviet prisoners faced a different but related danger. German authorities were already holding large numbers of captives from the summer battles in conditions of inadequate food, exposure and lethal violence. The prisoners' fate was not simply a matter of an army surprised by the quantity of men it had captured. Nazi policy treated Soviet soldiers as racially and ideologically inferior, and their custodians denied them protection and provision. This matters at the opening of an operation designed to produce another huge enclosure. The intended military result was the removal of Soviet armies from the field; for those captured, the consequence could be entry into a system that threatened their lives after their capacity to resist had ended.[7]

The wager on a short war

The attack on 30 September committed Guderian's force to the southern arm of a larger design. Its immediate purpose was to unhinge Bryansk Front; its strategic promise depended on the main attack, still two days away, defeating the armies farther north. Bock had concentrated enough strength to attempt another immense encirclement. Whether that would produce the political and military collapse Germany required was a separate question. Soviet armies, industrial resources and prospective foreign assistance remained outside the reach of the first thrust. The operation began by seeking to destroy a concentration of troops, but its planners expected that destruction to decide the future of a state. [1]

The German leaders had reasons for confidence. Their forces had won vast encirclement battles, and the main operational concentration was formidable. They also had reasons for concern that no declaration of intent could remove: losses, worn equipment, a long transport system, Soviet armies still capable of mobilising, and the need to secure a victory before their striking power deteriorated further. Soviet leaders faced a different mixture of capacity and danger. They possessed substantial forces west of Moscow but did not know the entire German attack as a completed pattern; they sought allied material help while preparing to fight with what was already at hand. Both sides made decisions under partial information. The German command's greater operational initiative did not give it knowledge of how the campaign would end.[1][6]

The first day's significance lay in that commitment. Germany was spending the strength assembled after Kiev on a new attempt to force a decision before a prolonged campaign demanded still more men and material. The Soviet command had to meet the blow with the armies already deployed while preserving the resources needed to replace losses. On 2 October, the northern and central arms of Typhoon would join the attack. For the moment, the new offensive was advancing from the south, and its ultimate success still depended on events that the opening movement could neither guarantee nor control. [1]
